evals.name: empty-argument-anaphora-default
evals.expected_output: With no topic named, the object is the assistant's own previous response. The skill re-reads that prior message, finds the part most likely to have lost the reader, and drops it to plain language — without asking 'explain what?' when the referent is obvious from the conversation.
expectations: Treats the empty argument as anaphora — the object is the ASSISTANT's previous output, not the user's, and not a re-prompt for a topic
Re-reads the prior assistant message this turn rather than recalling or guessing what was said
Does not ask 'explain what?' when the conversation makes the referent obvious

evals.name: plain-first-pass-concrete-analogy-zero-jargon
evals.expected_output: Lands at the lowest useful altitude first: one concrete everyday analogy, zero jargon, any unavoidable term defined inline. It leads with what the thing is actually doing, not with vocabulary, and does not open at peer level.
expectations: Opens at rung 1 (plain) with a concrete everyday analogy and zero unexplained jargon
Leads with the analogy and the 'what it's doing', not with a vocabulary dump; any unavoidable term is defined inline
Does not front-load the high-school or peer-level explanation

evals.name: altitude-climbs-only-on-request
evals.prompt: /education:explain the CAP theorem — and I already know distributed systems basics, give me the real version.
evals.expected_output: Altitude layering is on request. Because the user explicitly asks for the real version, the skill climbs toward peer level (rung 3) rather than staying at rung 1 plain — but the rungs are still offered as an invitation, not front-loaded across every response by default.
expectations: Recognizes the explicit request for higher altitude and climbs the rung ladder rather than staying pinned at rung 1
Treats altitude as request-driven — it does not default to dumping the peer-level explanation on an unqualified 'explain X'
Introduces real terms of art with definitions as altitude increases rather than assuming them silently
Rung-2 terms arrive as vocabulary-ladder entries: the term, an ordinary-words definition, and a modeled 'you can now say' sentence the user can reuse in their next prompt

evals.name: feynman-gap-check-surfaces-gap
evals.prompt: /education:explain simply why this proof of the Atiyah-Singer index theorem works
evals.expected_output: When the plain-language pass cannot shed the jargon without hand-waving, that is a detected understanding gap on the explainer's side. The skill surfaces it honestly — naming the specific part it cannot yet reduce and grounding harder — instead of emitting a confident-sounding restatement of jargon.
expectations: Runs the plain-language pass as a comprehension self-test, not a rewording service
When jargon cannot be shed, surfaces the specific gap honestly instead of papering over it with a confident restatement of the same jargon
Grounds harder (re-reads / fetches the source) before claiming to have explained it plainly

evals.name: closes-with-teach-handoff
evals.expected_output: After the one-shot explanation, it closes with a single lightweight line offering the multi-session path, /education:teach topic <x>, as the first-party sibling for ongoing coaching — one line, not a workspace pitch.
expectations: Closes the explanation with a lightweight offer of /education:teach for a multi-session deeper dive
Frames the handoff as one standard closing line, not a hard sell or a full workspace setup
Keeps the explanation itself one-shot — no persistent workspace, mission, or learning state is created

evals.name: auto-invokes-on-colloquial-trigger
evals.prompt: wait, what does this actually do?
evals.expected_output: The skill carries colloquial triggers and does not disable model invocation, so a bare 'what does this actually do' reaches it without an explicit command. It resolves the referent from context (anaphora) and drops it to plain language. Auto-trigger is best-effort; the explicit /education:explain path remains guaranteed.
expectations: Is eligible for model auto-invocation on a colloquial trigger (no disable-model-invocation) rather than requiring the explicit command
Resolves the referent from conversational context and delivers a plain-language explanation
Does not depend on the user naming the /education:explain command for the trigger to fire

evals.name: cold-start-empty-argument-asks-what
evals.expected_output: This is the first message in a new conversation — there is no prior assistant response to resolve the anaphora against. With nothing to drop to plain language, the skill does not hallucinate a referent or emit a confused response; it asks 'What would you like explained?' and waits for the user to name the object.
expectations: Detects that there is no prior assistant message in the conversation to treat as the anaphora referent
Asks 'What would you like explained?' (or equivalent) instead of proceeding blind or inventing a topic to explain
Does not hallucinate a referent or produce a confident plain-language explanation of something never stated

evals.name: original-ask-success-condition
evals.prompt: I'm trying to write a Postgres migration that adds a partial index but it keeps rejecting my syntax, and I don't get what "predicate" means in the docs. Explain it so I can fix my migration.
evals.expected_output: Lands a rung-1 plain explanation of a partial-index predicate (concrete analogy, jargon defined inline), aimed at unblocking the migration the user is stuck on. Because an original ask exists, the close shapes the vocabulary so the user's NEXT prompt can name what they mean (using "predicate" correctly), treating that next prompt as the success test rather than the explanation itself.
expectations: Recognizes the original ask behind the comprehension request and aims the explanation at unblocking it
Treats the user's next prompt as the success test: the close equips them to name what they mean (reusing the term correctly) rather than re-gesturing at the confusion
Still lands at rung 1 first with a concrete analogy and inline definitions

evals.name: starting-rung-default-plain
evals.prompt: /education:explain what a database transaction is [The repository has no docs/conventions/education.yaml. The education userConfig option explain_starting_rung is not set, so SKILL.md's userConfig line substitutes to its declared default, plain.]
evals.expected_output: explain_starting_rung resolves to plain at the default level, so the explanation opens at rung 1: one everyday analogy (for example a bank transfer that either moves the money or leaves both accounts as they were), no jargon, and the one-line offer of the next rung up. The reply ends with one line naming the value and the default level.
expectations: Opens at rung 1 with an everyday analogy and no undefined term of art
The rung offer names the high-school version, not the plain version
One line names explain_starting_rung as plain and the supplying level as the default

evals.name: starting-rung-userconfig-peer
evals.prompt: /education:explain what a database transaction is [No docs/conventions/education.yaml. The education userConfig option explain_starting_rung is set to peer, so SKILL.md's userConfig line substitutes to peer.]
evals.expected_output: The per-user level sets peer, so the explanation starts at rung 3: it opens with one precise sentence defining a transaction the way an engineer in the field would (a unit of work that commits all of its changes or none of them), then gives isolation, durability and the tradeoffs at full precision. It offers the plain version instead of a higher rung, and the last line names peer and the userConfig level.
expectations: The first sentence is a precise one-sentence definition using terms of art, not an everyday analogy
The body stays at peer level: real terms, edge cases or tradeoffs, no rung-1 analogy first
The one-line offer is for the plain version, not for a higher rung
One line names explain_starting_rung as peer from the userConfig level

evals.name: starting-rung-repo-file-wins-over-userconfig
evals.prompt: /education:explain what a mutex is [The repository's docs/conventions/education.yaml is captured in evals/fixtures/education-rung-plain.yaml relative to the skill directory. The education userConfig option explain_starting_rung is set to peer.]
evals.expected_output: Both levels set the key and the repository file wins: the value is plain from docs/conventions/education.yaml even though userConfig says peer. The explanation opens at rung 1 with an everyday analogy (one key to a single shared room), and the last line names plain and the repository file as the level.
expectations: The value resolves to plain from docs/conventions/education.yaml, not peer from userConfig
The explanation opens at rung 1 with an everyday analogy, not a precise peer-level definition
The reported level is the repository file

evals.name: starting-rung-invalid-repo-value-falls-back-to-default
evals.prompt: /education:explain what a mutex is [The repository's docs/conventions/education.yaml is captured in evals/fixtures/education-rung-invalid.yaml relative to the skill directory. The education userConfig option explain_starting_rung is set to peer.]
evals.expected_output: The repository file holds expert, which is not plain or peer. The run does not stop: it names docs/conventions/education.yaml, the key explain_starting_rung and the value expert, and drops that layer. No valid layer sits above it, so the key falls back to the default, plain; the lower userConfig value peer is not used in its place. The explanation then opens at rung 1.
expectations: Names the file docs/conventions/education.yaml, the key explain_starting_rung and the value expert as invalid
Still delivers an explanation; the invalid value does not stop the run
Resolves to plain at the default level, and does not fall through to the userConfig value peer
The explanation opens at rung 1 with an everyday analogy

evals.name: peer-start-offers-plain-version-not-higher-rung
evals.prompt: /education:explain what backpressure means in a message queue [The repository's docs/conventions/education.yaml is captured in evals/fixtures/education-rung-peer.yaml relative to the skill directory. The explain_starting_rung userConfig option substitutes to its default, plain.]
evals.expected_output: The repository file sets peer, which wins over the default. The reply opens with one precise sentence defining backpressure (a consumer signalling a producer to slow down when its buffer fills), ties it to the queue case at full precision, and closes the explanation with a single line offering the plain version. It does not offer a rung above peer, because rung 3 is the top of the ladder.
expectations: The opening is one precise sentence of definition, not an analogy
Exactly one line offers the plain version; no offer of a higher rung appears
The reported level is the repository file, with value peer

evals.name: codebase-subsystem-composes-explore-and-trace-intent
evals.prompt: /education:explain how our invoice retry scheduler works and why it waits so long between tries [This is a code repository. /discovery:explore and /discovery:trace-intent are among the available skills.]
evals.expected_output: The object is a codebase subsystem and the discovery skills are available, so the skill invokes /discovery:explore with --output explain for how the scheduler works and /discovery:trace-intent for why it waits, then explains from what they returned at the resolved starting rung. Where trace-intent marked a reason as inferred, the explanation keeps that hedge (appears to, likely) instead of stating it as fact.
expectations: Invokes /discovery:explore with --output explain for the how part
Invokes /discovery:trace-intent for the why part
A reason trace-intent graded Inferred or Unknown keeps its hedge or its not-found wording in the explanation; it is not restated as a confident fact

evals.name: codebase-subsystem-without-discovery-reads-files
evals.prompt: /education:explain how our invoice retry scheduler works [This is a code repository. Neither /discovery:explore nor /discovery:trace-intent is among the available skills.]
evals.expected_output: With the discovery skills unavailable, the skill does not try to invoke them. It grounds the explanation by reading the scheduler's files itself and cites the files it read. It does not claim why the scheduler was built that way unless a file it read states the reason.
expectations: Does not invoke or name /discovery:explore or /discovery:trace-intent as if they ran
Reads the scheduler's source files this turn and cites at least one file it read
Makes no claim about why a design choice was made unless a file it read states the reason

evals.name: no-framing-labels-or-pacing-narration
evals.expected_output: A plain explanation with no framing labels and no pacing narration: no 'Key insight:' or 'The big idea:' headings, no 'Let's pause here' or 'Take a moment to think', no 'Step 1 of 3' progress lines, no say-it-back request and no quiz. The one-line offer of the next rung and the /education:teach handoff line are kept.
expectations: Contains no framing label such as 'Key insight', 'The big idea' or 'Bottom line' introducing a sentence
Contains no pacing narration such as 'let's pause', 'take a moment' or step-of-total progress lines
Asks no comprehension question and requests no say-it-back
Keeps exactly one rung-offer line and the /education:teach handoff line
